title: AI search tools marketers should know in 2026
content:
Something big just shifted in how people find answers online.
More buyers are skipping the investigation and deliberation of clicking through blue links on Google, in favor of asking ChatGPT, Perplexity, and the like for one direct answer.
That changes everything for us marketers. The question is no longer just “Do we rank?” It’s “Do AI search tools even mention us?” This guide breaks down what AI search tools actually are, how buyers are using them today, and which tools belong in your stack as a marketer.
An AI search tool or AI search software is any application that uses artificial intelligence to help users crawl, find, retrieve, or synthesize information. But that’s a broad net covering various tools for research, visibility, and optimization.
These three categories—research, visibility, and optimization—often get lumped together, but they shouldn’t be. Knowing which type of tool you’re dealing with helps you determine which tool actually fits your needs. We’ll dig into that more shortly.
Buyers have always done research before making a purchase. What’s changed is where and how far along they get before a vendor ever hears from them.
The numbers speak volumes. Forrester found that 94% of B2B buyers used AI during recent purchase processes. Of those, 55% used AI to compare vendors, 54% to research products, and 47% to build internal business cases, all before talking to a single sales rep.
AI answer engines now rank as the #1 source for vendor research, ahead of vendor websites, sales reps, and product experts.
On the other end, McKinsey research found that about 50% of consumers across all demographics (including boomers) use AI-powered search for purchasing decisions. In fact, Adobe Digital Insights reported that 56% of US consumers used generative AI during the 2025 holiday shopping season, up 45% from the year prior.
By the time a buyer fills out your demo request form or replies to outreach, they’ve likely already consulted an AI engine with many of their questions. According to Forrester, AI answer engines are now the #1 vendor research source, and the buying journey is largely complete before any vendor contact happens.
For marketers, the old playbook of “rank on Google, get traffic” is no longer enough. Visibility inside answer engines is becoming the primary discovery layer, especially for purchase-intent queries.
Before comparing specific products, it helps to understand the three main categories. Each serves a different person with a different goal.
Answer engines are the ChatGPTs and Geminis of the world. Users ask them questions in plain language and get synthesized answers crafted by the tools, drawing from multiple sources.
Some cite their sources; some don’t. Some are real-time and web-connected; some rely on training data. Either way, the goal is to give the user a single response, not just use semantic search to deliver resources to filter through, as with a traditional search engine.
Buyers use answer engines for discovery, comparison, and follow-up research. At the same time, HubSpot’s AI Trends Report found 40% of marketers turn to them for research, data analysis, and content generation, among other things . (This also makes them the most popular AI tool among marketers.)
Marketers can’t control what answer engines say about them to consumers, but they can influence it through answer engine optimization or sharing credible, well-sourced content that answer engines cite.
Ever landed on a clothing website looking for something specific? The search bar at the top of that site is an example of an AI site search tool.
AI site search tools are embedded into a company’s website, app, or internal knowledge base. They help users find relevant pages, products, or answers without leaving the page. Platforms like Algolia , Coveo , and Elasticsearch fall in this bucket.
AI site search tools matter most for SaaS companies, e-commerce brands, and enterprises with large content libraries. If visitors can’t find what they’re looking for on your site, they’ll ask an answer engine instead.
AEO tools are marketer-facing platforms and arguably the fastest-growing of the three AI search tool categories. They track how often your brand appears in AI-generated answers, compare your visibility against competitors, and give you recommendations to close the gap.
For more details, see our guide to the best AI search analytics tools for marketing teams .
According to Bain & Company , 60% of searches now end without a click, and AI search is a major contributor to that trend. The brands that show up in AI-generated answers are the ones buyers actually see.
When selecting an AI search tool, the best choice is one that fits the specific job you’re trying to do, not just the one that’s most popular or has the most features.
Let’s break down the best AI search tools with the common marketing use cases in mind.
Note: AI is a market that is still evolving, and many of these tools have shortcomings and controversies. Evaluate them closely before using and remember to use them as strategic tools, not replacements for human creativity and discretion.
Unlike most AI search tools you hear about today, this one’s just for us marketers. We marketers need to know whether our brand is showing up in the tools consumers use to search.
HubSpot AEO is built specifically for this job, tracking brand visibility across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, while also monitoring emerging AI search tools like Google’s AI search features .
HubSpot AEO is differentiated from standalone AEO tools like RankPrompt by using data from your CRM to predict the prompts your actual buyers are most likely to type. Instead of starting from generic industry guesses, it grounds recommendations in what HubSpot already knows about your specific customers and business.
Customers using the AEO beta and prioritizing answer engines saw A I referral traffic grow 20% , even as overall organic traffic fell 27% year-over-year.
Best for: HubSpot customers; Marketers who want ongoing visibility tracking, competitor benchmarking, citation analysis, and actionable recommendations across the major answer engines.
Pricing: Available with Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise, or as a standalone at $50/month.
Not sure where to start? HubSpot’s AI Search Grader offers a free , one-time diagnostic snapshot of how your brand appears in AI search results. It’s a lightweight first step before committing to ongoing tracking.
If you need a research partner for everyday questions, competitive intel, content brainstorming, or quick synthesis, ChatGPT is the most widely recognized and used option by a wide margin. In fact, our research found that even 88% of marketers have used it in their roles, beating Gemini, which ranked second, by a whopping 33%.
ChatGPT processes more than 2.5 billion prompts per day , according to OpenAI data. It handles everything from creative writing and market research to coding and multi-step analysis.
Research from Bain & Company found that 68% of LLM users rely on these platforms to research, gather, and summarize information, and 42% use them for shopping recommendations .
Best for: Marketers, writers, and researchers who want a versatile AI assistant for open-ended research, drafting, and synthesis.
Pricing: Free tier available. ChatGPT Plus at $20/month.
Pro tip: HubSpot has a deep research connector with ChatGPT, which lets you bring your CRM customer data into the tool and act on those insights.
At Bloomberg’s Tech Summit, CEO Aravind Srinivas revealed Perplexity processed 780 million queries in May 2025 alone, with over 20% month-over-month growth. It’s particularly popular with B2B buyers doing deep vendor evaluations, and it’s easy to see why.
On the surface, Perplexity looks very similar to ChatGPT, but it was built from the ground up around real-time, sourced answers. Unlike ChatGPT, every Perplexity response comes with inline citations. Sources are a first-class part of the interface, not an afterthought, which is essential for credibility.
According to the Columbia Journalism Review , which tested eight AI search tools on citation accuracy, Perplexity had the lowest error rate at 37%. That’s not perfect, but it makes Perplexity the most reliable option at the moment.
Best for: Any task where accuracy and sourcing are paramount — Fact-checking, competitive research, academic or technical topics.
Pricing: Free tier available. Perplexity Pro at $20/month.
If the problem is that visitors can’t find what they need on your website or that employees can’t sort through your internal documentation, you may need an AI site search tool, not an answer engine.
Algolia is the go-to for speed and developer flexibility. It powers search for websites and applications with strong e-commerce and SaaS use cases.
Algolia has also recently expanded into generative AI with its NeuralSearch and Ask AI features.
Coveo is stronger for enterprises with complex knowledge bases, Salesforce or SAP integrations, and personalized recommendations across customer-facing portals.
If your team is on Salesforce or SAP, Coveo’s native connectors remove a significant setup burden that other tools require custom engineering to solve.
Best for: E-commerce sites, SaaS documentation portals, large knowledge bases, and enterprise intranets that need smarter, AI-powered internal search.
The AI search tool landscape is noisy. New entrants are launching constantly, and feature checklists can look very similar on the surface.
Here’s what actually matters when you’re evaluating a tool:
Not exactly. While many AI search tools incorporate chat-based interfaces, not all chatbots are AI. The defining feature of an AI search tool is information retrieval.
AI search tools are designed to help you find, synthesize, or act on information, while chatbots are more focused on conversation, task completion, or customer service. ChatGPT, Gemini, and other similar tools sit at the intersection of both: they’re conversational AIs that also perform powerful research and search tasks.
AI search tools are what individual users interact with directly to find information, such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Claude, and so on, for a variety of different purposes.
AEO tools are what marketers use to track and improve how their brand appears inside those AI search tools. They’re on opposite sides of the same equation: one is the channel, the other is the measurement and optimization layer for that channel.
Traditional search analytics don’t capture AI search visibility.
You won’t find a “ChatGPT Search Console” or a Perplexity ranking report. AEO tools fill this gap by sending test prompts to answer engines, recording whether and how a brand appears, and tracking changes over time.
HubSpot AEO does this across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, using CRM data to prioritize the prompts most likely to reflect real buyer behavior. HubSpot Marketing also includes “AI referrals” as a traffic source.
For a quick starting point, HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader delivers a one-time diagnostic snapshot with no setup required.
AI site search matters most when users are already on your website or inside your product and trying to find something specific. If your site has a large content library, complex documentation, or a product catalog, a smart internal search experience directly affects engagement, conversion, and support costs.
If users can’t find what they need on your site, they’re more likely to leave and ask an external answer engine, which may or may not send them back. Investing in AI site search (with tools like Algolia or Coveo) is about keeping qualified visitors in your ecosystem once they arrive.
AI search is moving fast. The good news is that the fundamentals of credible content, transparent sourcing, and strong brand authority still apply. The new requirement is measurement. Knowing where your brand stands in answer engines is the first step toward improving your visibility in these channels.
Answer engines have become the first stop for B2B buyers comparing vendors, consumers researching products, and just about everyone with a question they’d rather not dig through 10 links to find the answer. Most marketers know this, but fewer are actually doing anything about it yet. This is your advantage.
The tools in this article cover three specific functions: answer engines for day-to-day research, AI site search to keep your own visitors engaged, and AEO tools to measure and improve how your brand appears in answer engines. You don’t need all of them at once. Start with the tool that addresses your most immediate need.
If you’re a marketer and you’re not yet tracking your brand’s visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Gemini, that’s the gap worth closing first. Start with HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader to see where you stand, then use HubSpot AEO to track it over time.
The search for the right tools is over. Now is the time to act.

title: How Local Businesses Can Build Visibility In AI Search via @sejournal, @lorenbaker
content:
I recently had the pleasure of hosting the opening session of SEJ Live with Kevin Chen and Jonathan Berthold from Moz, the sponsors of the session. Kevin, the VP of Business Development, and Jonathan, the VP of Revenue, shared valuable insights during the session.
We made the most of our hour by focusing on questions attendees submitted beforehand. Here’s a summary of our engaging discussion. You can also catch the full session for free over here.
Jonathan started with a definition that described AI visibility for a local business as being the company an assistant recommends when someone describes what they want. He told a story about a talented tattoo artist friend and sees people moving past “best tattoo artist” in ChatGPT or Gemini and asking instead for the best artist for a specific style of line work.
The model can now access a wider range of sources than ever, extending beyond basic map packs. It gathers information from listings, review sites, Reddit threads, city forums, and curated local website lists to improve its responses. For instance, one citation supporting his friend’s suggestion was from a hotel website featuring a list of local artists.
Jonathan started in SEO in 2010, when local was a checklist of directories. His estimate is that the work has roughly tripled since then, because a model can pull a mention from anywhere, including wherever your competitors are earning theirs.
Kevin reminded us that the fundamentals are always key, no matter how much technology evolves. It’s really important to maintain consistency with your name, address, phone number, and hours across all platforms. Plus, your website should be easy to read and well-organized so models can easily find the information they need. In his view, the site is now the source the models draw on more than the place customers go to read about you. That’s why keeping your data current is more important than ever.
https://cdn.searchenginejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/clip_05_Googles_April_2025_Rule_Killed_Scripted_Review_Requests_short.mp4
For years, the common advice was to ask customers to share the service they received and the name of the person who helped them. Jonathan pointed out that Google changed its Maps content policy in April, and now it’s no longer allowed. Merchants can’t have staff request a set number of reviews or ask for reviews mentioning specific details, like a staff member’s name. So, the staff leaderboard and “mention me” cards are a thing of the past.
Making things easier for customers really makes a positive impact. For instance, Jonathan’s barber has a handy sign with a QR code that takes customers straight to their Google Business Profile, and a link on the invoice does the same job. Without an easy path to your profile somewhere along the way, asking for reviews gets hard fast, even when the service earns them.
I’ve been thinking about how people sometimes feel overwhelmed by review requests. Just recently, after spending an afternoon receiving prompts from a restaurant, a mobile game, a bank, and another app – all asking for reviews – I realized how much review fatigue can really take its toll. Jonathan agreed that this is a genuine concern and shared that a kind, gentle request often works better than multiple follow-up emails. Kevin also added that recent reviews are especially important to him. When he’s searching for an apartment, for example, he tends to skip past negative reviews from three years ago and instead pays close attention to what current reviewers are saying.
Jonathan said to respond to everything, positive and negative, and Julie gave a really helpful explanation in the chat, making things clearer. When replying to a negative review, remember that it’s for everyone who reads the exchange later, more than for the reviewer. Jonathan recommends acknowledging any frustration, reassuring them that we’re actively working on the issue behind the scenes, and sharing contact details like a phone number or email for more support. It’s always best to stay respectful and avoid getting into arguments in the comments. Kevin pointed out that response time is very important, and the number of reviews probably matters less than how fast we answer the ones with something to say. Google also highlights in its local ranking tips that having more reviews and positive ratings can improve our standing, and lists replying to reviews among its tips.
I first got involved with franchises in local search when the map pack was just beginning to emerge. Since it took some time for the head office to develop a clear plan, location managers got impatient and launched their own MySpace pages and answered their own Yelp reviews. Swap in Instagram and TikTok and the same thing is happening now.
Jonathan suggests that having a unified brand strategy is the way to go – then you can meet your customers right where they are. What works well in bustling New York City might not be the best fit in Wichita, and the same goes for whether each location should have its own social media profile. He mentioned that it really depends on whether each location has something unique to share.
If your social team doesn’t know what the review team’s doing, and the review team doesn’t know what the data team’s doing, you’re actually going to lose the race.
He thinks listings, reviews, and social are coming back together because the AI agents handling them can talk to each other. He compared adoption to a self-driving car. Watch what it recommends, build trust, then let it run.
During summer vacation, I saw a lively crowd outside a popular burger restaurant that had gone viral on TikTok, while the burger place across the street sat empty. When the food arrived, the patty was sliding off the bun, and the bacon undercooked, and the same people who filmed themselves waiting in line began filming themselves being let down.
That’s why I find reviews very useful for learning. Kevin pointed out that sentiment analysis tools can identify common themes, which I find interesting. For example, if “food” is the most frequently mentioned word in a restaurant’s reviews, it doesn’t tell the whole story unless you also consider how many of those mentions are negative. Jonathan suggests we go a step further by setting up tracked prompts built on the business name, asking the models what people think of it and what it could improve. You can fix the thing customers keep complaining about long before you can fix a missing citation.
A school chain I collaborated with kept hearing from prospective students who had been misled by Google’s AI. Google’s AI had told them tuition was several thousand dollars lower than it was, and the source was a Reddit post from years earlier that AI Overviews was citing. I also shared a more detailed account of this on the podcast with Kris Jones.
Finding it is what tracking is for. Jonathan noted that Reddit citations in ChatGPT were down recently, one engine over one window, as he put it. The tracking data behind that is from mid-August, and the firm that published it says the numbers could still move. Old threads keep collecting new comments because they stay visible in search, so posting an update in the thread, or asking the moderators to correct it, is worth a try.
My connection dropped near the end, so Heather Campbell kindly stepped in to manage the Q&A. The main question was what to investigate first when a business ranks number one on Google but doesn’t appear in AI search results. Jonathan would run prompts across several engines to identify which businesses and URLs are cited, then verifies whether AI crawlers can access the site. He has observed cases where outdated robots.txt rules from previous webmasters unintentionally blocked AI crawlers.
When Carmen asked about sharing this information with leadership, both answers were the same word, conversion. It’s helpful to encourage tracking calls and direction requests by source and to watch whether revenue moves.

title: Google DeepMind Develops New AI Search Ranking Model via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
Google recently published a research paper about training an LLM to replace current back-end ranking architectures for search. The researchers propose using Autoregressive Ranking as a replacement for the current two-stage ranking systems.
In a very general and plain English sense, traditional search ranking systems typically have a two-stage architecture with a Dual Encoder and a Cross Encoder.
Dual Encoders are efficient and fast but are limited in how precisely they can rank documents. That’s why ranking systems use Cross Encoders, which are more powerful. But Cross Encoders are too computationally expensive for large-scale retrieval, which is why they’re used in the second stage for ranking the candidate documents.
What the researchers are proposing is replacing the two-stage search retrieval back-end with a new system called Autoregressive Ranking (ARR). The research paper is titled Autoregressive Ranking: Bridging the Gap Between Dual and Cross Encoders . The researchers are from Google DeepMind, University of Massachusetts Amherst, and The University of Texas at Austin.
It’s a fairly radical change to replace the standard two-stage ranking system with a single LLM that produces the ranked list of documents. Should something like this be used, the implications for SEO/AEO would be profound.
The first step of creating the ranking model is to train it. The researchers developed a method called SToICaL (Simple Token-Item Calibrated Loss) to teach an LLM how to rank documents.
The training teaches the LLM which documents should rank higher and lower in two ways:
The result is an LLM that learns which documents are relevant and is able to suppress ranking of irrelevant ones.
“We then propose SToICaL (Simple Token-Item Calibrated Loss), a generalized rank-aware training loss for LLM finetuning. By using item-level reweighting and prefix-tree marginalization, we distribute probability mass over valid docID tokens based on their ground-truth relevance.”
The researchers tested their new system to evaluate whether it actually improves ranking performance versus ordinary next-token prediction, using two datasets, WordNet and ESCI Shopping Queries. They also compared it to standard Dual Encoders and Cross Encoders in a separate test using WordNet.
The results of the testing showed that Autoregressive Ranking (ARR) performed strongly but not across all metrics.
One area that needs further research is that, in the shopping-search test, one version of the method became worse at ranking the most relevant result first, even though it improved the overall ranking of the results.
The researchers conclude that Dual Encoders (DEs) become constrained as the number of documents to rank grows because, in order to represent every possible ranking, the vector size has to correspondingly grow. They show that ARR does not have that limitation and in theory it can rank an arbitrary number of documents.
“We provide a theoretical foundation for the superior expressive capacity of ARR over DEs. A rigorous analysis of the embedding geometry required for ranking shows that for a DE to achieve any ordering of 𝑘 documents, its embedding dimension must grow linearly with 𝑘.
In contrast, we prove that an ARR model with constant hidden dimension is theoretically sufficient to rank an arbitrary number of documents. This offers a formal explanation for the advantages of ARR.”
However, this is a theoretical result, meaning that it does not necessarily establish that ARR will perform this way in real-world search systems. Yet the researchers also say that their experiments showed the approach improved ranking performance and became better at keeping irrelevant documents below relevant ones.
“In this paper, we established a theoretical foundation for Autoregressive Ranking, proving that while DEs require embedding dimensions to grow with corpus size, ARR models generating multi-token docIDs can solve complete ranking tasks with a constant hidden dimension, given a mild condition on the rank of the embedding matrix for the docID tokens.
We proposed a generalized rank-aware training loss for (pointwise) autoregressive ranking that relies on item-level reweighting and prefixtree marginalization to distribute probability mass over valid docID tokens based on their ground-truth relevance. Experiments on WordNet and ESCI show this approach successfully suppresses invalid docID generations and improves on key ranking metrics.”
